about: Closed vocabulary for atomic ritual acts. Each step's `atoms[]` decomposes it into verb(theme, roles). Atoms are the comparable layer; unitIds remain the source-bound phrase layer. `effect` drives derived object lifecycles: introduce = the theme enters the rite; consume = the theme leaves it; transform = the theme becomes `result`; charge = the theme receives the unwanted condition and must later be disposed of; use = no lifecycle change.

bring.gloss: bring a thing or being into the ritual space

select.gloss: choose a person or animal for a role

collect.gloss: take a substance from a place

take.gloss: take hold of / take up an object already present

carry.gloss: carry an object along a path

combine.gloss: join materials into one (twist, mix, blend)

shape.gloss: form material into an object (wreath, figure, loaf)

crush.gloss: crush, grind or pound a material

wind.gloss: wind thread or cord around X

detach.gloss: remove X from a person, animal or object

position.gloss: seat, turn or station a person

hold-over.gloss: raise or wave X over a person so it takes up the condition

press.gloss: press a substance against the body so it absorbs the condition

present.gloss: raise X toward a deity or show it

draw-out.gloss: pull X out of the body or an orifice

anoint.gloss: smear or rub a substance on

apply.gloss: apply a remedy to the body (bandage, poultice, daub)

ingest.gloss: eat or drink (the patient takes a remedy or meal)

comb.gloss: draw a comb or object downward over the body

touch.gloss: lay hold of a living exemplar or object

gesture.gloss: bow, kneel, raise hands or perform a bodily sign

pass.gloss: a person moves through or between a boundary

observe.gloss: watch for a sign (birds, dream, oracle)

dedicate.gloss: assign an animal or thing to a deity

offer.gloss: set food or goods before a deity or power

scatter.gloss: strew over the ground or road

bury.gloss: bury or deposit in the ground

drive.gloss: send an animal or person along a path

release.gloss: let go into water, open country or foreign territory

close.gloss: shut a door or seal a container

speak.gloss: an utterance; its kind is given by `act`

speechActs.invocation: call a deity or power by name to attend
speechActs.petition: ask a deity or power for a good
speechActs.appeasement: ask an angry deity to be calm, satisfied, or reconciled
speechActs.confession: acknowledge a fault that caused the harm
speechActs.assignment: declare that X belongs to, or is for, Y
speechActs.substitution: declare that X takes the place of a person
speechActs.dismissal: tell the harm, or the god who sent it, to go
speechActs.analogy: as X, so may Y (a comparison that performs the change)
speechActs.declaration: state that the change has happened ("I have cleansed him")
speechActs.binding: call for a harmful power to be seized, bound or held
speechActs.accusation: lay a case against the harm or its maker before a divine judge

objectClasses.body: a part of a participant's body
objectClasses.harm: an abstract unwanted condition (plague, impurity, sorcery, anger)
objectClasses.ornament: a ring, bead, wreath or other adornment
objectClasses.food: bread, grain, fruit, cheese, fodder or other food
objectClasses.drink: wine, beer, milk, honey or other drinkable liquid
objectClasses.liquid: water, oil or other non-drink liquid
objectClasses.fat: fat, tallow or wax as a substance
objectClasses.meat: meat or parts of a killed animal
objectClasses.structure: a gate, hut, hearth, door or table
objectClasses.plant: a plant, herb, wood or aromatic
objectClasses.place: a location treated as a participant (river, spring, road)
objectClasses.materials: the used materials of the rite taken together

elimination.label: sending the trouble away on a carrier
elimination.reading: Something unwanted should leave the person or group: it is loaded onto a carrier (animal, figure, object) that is then sent off or destroyed.
elimination.boundary: Do not invent an enemy or a sender of the trouble. The carrier's destination can be adapted to 'away, out of bounds'.

slots.why: A carrier is chosen first because the rite needs something that can leave in the person's place: the ram of Uḫḫamuwa and Ašḫella, the substitutes and bull of Puliša, the clay figure riding donkeys in the li'bu-fever rite.

Adorning the carrier marks it out for the power it will reach. Uḫḫamuwa crowns the ram with a five-coloured wreath and Ašḫella binds wool and metal rings to its horns, so the god receives something fit to accept.
This is the moment of transfer. Holding the carrier over the body, pressing it against the limbs, or declaring it a substitute moves the trouble from the person onto the carrier.
Speech makes the direction explicit: the trouble, or the god behind it, is told to go and not return. The words fix where the loaded carrier is headed.
The carrier now holds the trouble, so it cannot stay. Driving it to another land, releasing it into a river, burning or burying it ends the transfer.

stripping.label: stripping off and washing away
stripping.reading: A clinging condition is taken off the person piece by piece: coverings removed, body washed or combed, used materials sent away.
stripping.boundary: A modern obstacle is an analogy, not a historical impurity.

slots.why: The condition is treated as something that clings: Tunnawiya slits the black shirt and pulls wool from the patient's body, and Puliša draws coloured wool out of the king's mouth. Taking it off takes the condition with it.
Washing follows removal, so what remains on the body is cleaned away rather than covered over.
A declaration or dismissal names what has been taken off, so the change is spoken as well as done.
What was stripped off still carries the condition. The sources send it into the river or the fire rather than keep it.

passage.label: passage into a new condition
passage.reading: The person crosses from one state or phase to another: entering a new place, role, or chapter of life.
passage.boundary: The gate or fires express the change; do not claim the source concerned the modern transition.

slots.why: A threshold is built or kindled first: Paškuwatti's reed gate, Tunnawiya's alanza-wood gate, Ašḫella's two fires. The crossing needs a boundary to cross.
Binding the gate with coloured wool marks it as a ritual boundary rather than an ordinary doorway.
Passing through is the central act: the person leaves one condition on one side and arrives in the next on the other.
Something handed over or put on at the threshold makes the new condition visible. Paškuwatti takes the spindle and distaff and gives a bow and arrows.
The words state what the crossing means. At the alanza gate Tunnawiya compares it to the thousands of herdsmen the gate has purified.

increase.label: increase by comparison
increase.reading: A desired good should grow: a flourishing exemplar (fruit tree, fertile animal) is touched or shown and the wish is spoken 'as this, so may that'.
increase.boundary: Fertility comparisons are adapted by analogy; do not add a wish for children.

slots.why: A flourishing example is touched or shown first. Tunnawiya takes hold of a cow by the horn and of a fruit-bearing tree, so the comparison has something real before it.
The comparison performs the wish: as this tree bears fruit, as this cow fills her pen, so may the desired good increase.

provision.label: giving to win a favourable response
provision.reading: Something valued is provided to a power whose goodwill matters, and a favourable response is asked in return.
provision.boundary: Preserve the source recipient; food in an offering does not make a deity a patron of a modern business.

slots.why: Goods are gathered first because the rite works by giving: fodder for a god's horses, bread, wine and cheese for the god of the road.
Preparing the gift makes it fit for its recipient before it is handed over.
Offering, pouring or strewing places the gift before the power whose goodwill is sought.
The request follows the gift. Ancient offerings set up reciprocity: something is given, then something is asked.

appeasement.label: calming an angry power
appeasement.reading: A relationship has soured; the offended party is fed, honoured and asked to turn back toward peace.
appeasement.boundary: A modern person is never identified with a deity; the rite asks divine aid concerning the relationship.

slots.why: Anger is first met with provision: Uḫḫamuwa sends fodder and tallow for the angry god's horses and chariot.
Naming the fault, as Muršili does in the plague prayer, acknowledges the cause before asking for the anger to end.
The appeal asks the offended power to be calm and turn back toward peace.

protection.label: setting a boundary against harm
protection.reading: A person, house or group is shielded: a boundary is marked or sealed and harm is declared to stay outside.
protection.boundary: Competition alone is not a demand to harm a rival.

slots.why: The boundary is marked or sealed: a door anointed, a deposit buried at the gate, wool bound on the threshold.
The words say what the boundary does: harm stays outside, good stays within.

transformation.label: changing identity or role
transformation.reading: The person puts off one role and takes up another: garments or implements are exchanged and the new state is declared.
transformation.boundary: Source gender roles are historical particulars; the adaptation concerns the change, not a gender claim.

slots.why: The old role is set down first, as the king takes off his festive garments or the offerant hands back the spindle.
Something new is put on or taken up, so the new role has a visible form.
A declaration or comparison states the change, so the new role is named as well as worn.

healing.label: preparing and taking a remedy
healing.reading: A condition of body or mind is treated: ingredients are gathered, prepared and applied or taken until recovery.
healing.boundary: This is a historical recipe presented for interest, never medical advice; the adapted version must not be ingested.

slots.why: The remedy begins with its ingredients: named plants, oils, honey, stones.
Crushing, mixing and boiling turn separate ingredients into one remedy.
The remedy is applied or taken. Here it is shown for its form only, never to be used.
An incantation or declaration often closes the treatment in both Hittite and Babylonian recipes.

return.label: sending harm back to its source
return.reading: Harm that someone caused is returned to them: figures stand for the harm or its maker and are presented, bound and destroyed.
return.boundary: Never name or target a real person; the rite returns the condition, not injury to an individual.

slots.why: Figures stand for the harm or for its maker, so the harm has a form that can be acted on.
The figures, or the afflicted person, are set before the divine judge, usually the Sun-god.
The words send the harm back to where it came from and ask the judge to rule on it.
Winding thread around the figures holds the returned harm fast.
Destroying the figures completes the return: they are crushed, melted or burned.

sign.label: seeking a sign or answer
sign.reading: An answer about the future or a decision is sought: signs are watched, or the person sleeps over a deposit to receive one.
sign.boundary: Present the result as the rite's form, never as a prediction.

slots.why: A deposit is set in place first, as Allii's basket is placed beneath the bed.
The answer is waited for: the person sleeps over the deposit, or birds are watched.
The question is put to the power who will answer it.

petition.label: a direct appeal
petition.reading: A power is addressed directly: named, honoured and asked for the particular good.
petition.boundary: A modern person is never identified with a deity.

slots.why: The power is approached with a gift or a gesture before it is addressed.
Calling the power by name asks for its attention.
The request itself: the particular good is named.
A promise of return, as in Muršili's vow, completes the exchange.

why.opening: This act opens the rite before its central operation, as washing or an invocation opens many of the source rituals.
why.closing: This act closes the rite after its central operation, as a libation or a final word often does in the sources.
why.dispose: Whatever has taken up the unwanted condition must leave the rite. This act removes it.
why.manual: You added this step by hand.
why.attested: This act comes from a ritual that was performed for the aim you asked about. The sequence follows the order of the tablet, with animals replaced by figures and nothing to be eaten.
